countries.name: Georgia
countries.summary: Georgia, between the Black Sea and the Caspian on the southern slopes of the Caucasus, is one of the oldest wine countries on earth: archaeologists have found traces of winemaking there from about 6000 BC. Its signature is the qvevri, a large clay vessel buried in the ground, in which whites are often fermented and aged on their skins to make amber wines. Kakheti in the east makes most of the wine, from Saperavi, a red grape with red flesh, and Rkatsiteli, a white. Georgia names many of its wines for villages, and several well loved reds are semi-sweet.
countries.overview:
Wine is woven into Georgian life: the vine appears in its churches and its legends, and the supra, the feast led by a toastmaster, is unthinkable without it. Vines have grown here since the Neolithic, and more than five hundred native grape varieties are recorded, though only a few dozen are planted commercially.

The traditional winemaking uses the qvevri, an egg-shaped clay vessel lined with beeswax and buried up to its neck, so the wine ferments and rests at a steady, cool temperature. In the Kakhetian way, white grapes are crushed into the qvevri with their skins, and often their stems, and left for months, making amber wines with tannin, dried fruit and nutty notes. In the west, in Imereti, only part of the skins goes in. UNESCO added qvevri winemaking to its list of intangible cultural heritage in 2013.

Under Soviet rule Georgia supplied sweet and semi-sweet wine in bulk to the Soviet market, and quality and the old methods suffered. Since independence in 1991, and especially after a Russian embargo from 2006 pushed producers towards new markets, small family wineries have revived qvevri wine alongside modern wines made in steel and oak.

Georgian wine law protects places of origin. The protected names include Tsinandali, Mukuzani, Kindzmarauli and Khvanchkara, each tied to a place, a grape or grapes and a style, and the National Wine Agency oversees them. For the exam, know the qvevri, Kakheti, Saperavi and Rkatsiteli, and the semi-sweet reds.

A broader regional name, such as Kakheti, with looser rules.
Wine named only for Georgia or for a grape.

places.name: Kakheti
places.note: The eastern heartland in the Alazani valley under the Greater Caucasus, source of most of the country's wine and of its classic qvevri whites.

places.name: Tsinandali
places.note: A dry white blend led by Rkatsiteli with Mtsvane, named for a village and an old estate in the Telavi district.

places.name: Mukuzani
places.note: A dry red from Saperavi, aged in oak, from the right bank of the Alazani river.

places.name: Kindzmarauli
places.note: A semi-sweet red from Saperavi grown near Kvareli, its fermentation stopped by cold to keep natural sugar.

places.name: Akhasheni
places.note: Another semi-sweet red from Saperavi, from the Gurjaani district of Kakheti.

places.name: Kartli
places.note: The central region around Tbilisi, cooler than Kakheti, known for Chinuri and Goruli Mtsvane and for traditional method sparkling wine.

places.name: Imereti
places.note: The western region where wine is fermented with only part of the skins, giving lighter amber whites from Tsolikouri, Tsitska and Krakhuna.

places.name: Racha-Lechkhumi
places.note: A mountainous western region whose Khvanchkara is a naturally semi-sweet red from Aleksandrouli and Mujuretuli.

grapes.name: Saperavi
grapes.styles: A teinturier with red flesh, making deep, fresh dry reds and the semi-sweet reds of Kakheti.

grapes.name: Rkatsiteli
grapes.styles: The most planted white, crisp in steel and tannic and amber when made on its skins in qvevri.

grapes.name: Mtsvane
grapes.styles: Kakhuri Mtsvane, an aromatic white that freshens Rkatsiteli in Tsinandali and makes fine amber wines alone.

grapes.name: Kisi
grapes.styles: A Kakhetian white revived for rich, apricot scented qvevri wines.

grapes.name: Aleksandrouli
grapes.styles: A red of Racha, blended with Mujuretuli for the semi-sweet Khvanchkara.

exam: Describe the qvevri and the Kakhetian method of skin contact.
Know Saperavi as a red-fleshed grape and Rkatsiteli as the main white.
Tie Tsinandali, Mukuzani, Kindzmarauli and Khvanchkara to their grapes and styles.
Place Kakheti in the east and Imereti in the west.
traps: Kindzmarauli and Khvanchkara are semi-sweet reds, not dry.
Amber wine is a white made on its skins, not a rosé.
Georgia the country is not the American state; its key in the Codex is the country.

cards.b: The qvevri, an egg-shaped clay jar lined with beeswax and buried to its neck.
White grapes fermented and aged for months in qvevri with their skins and often stems, making amber wine.

cards.f: Saperavi: what is unusual about it?
cards.b: It is a teinturier: its flesh is red, so its wines are deeply coloured.
A dry white blend led by Rkatsiteli with Mtsvane, from Kakheti.
A naturally semi-sweet red from Saperavi, grown near Kvareli in Kakheti.
Kakheti, in the east, in the Alazani valley.
A semi-sweet red from Aleksandrouli and Mujuretuli, grown in Racha-Lechkhumi.

questions.q: What is the Georgian clay vessel buried in the ground for fermenting wine called?
questions.exp: The qvevri is the buried clay vessel of Georgia; the tinaja is Spanish, the dolium Roman and the pithos Greek.

questions.q: Which red grape with red flesh leads Georgian red wine?
questions.exp: Saperavi is a teinturier with red flesh; Rkatsiteli, Mtsvane and Kisi are white grapes.

questions.q: In which region is most Georgian wine made?
questions.exp: Kakheti, in the east along the Alazani valley, makes most of the wine of the country; Imereti and Guria lie in the west, Kartli in the centre.

questions.q: What is a Georgian white wine fermented on its skins commonly called?
questions.exp: Georgians call a white fermented on its skins amber wine; the same style is known elsewhere as orange wine.

questions.q: Which dry white blend is led by Rkatsiteli with Mtsvane?
questions.exp: Tsinandali is a dry white of Rkatsiteli and Mtsvane; Mukuzani is a dry red, and Kindzmarauli and Khvanchkara are semi-sweet reds.

questions.q: Which grape is the main white of Georgia?
questions.exp: Rkatsiteli is the most planted white of Georgia, made both fresh in steel and amber in qvevri.

questions.q: Which semi-sweet red comes from Aleksandrouli and Mujuretuli grapes in Racha-Lechkhumi?
questions.exp: Khvanchkara is the naturally semi-sweet red of Racha; Kindzmarauli and Akhasheni are semi-sweet reds of Saperavi in Kakheti, and Mukuzani is dry.

questions.q: In which year did UNESCO add qvevri winemaking to its intangible heritage list?
questions.exp: UNESCO inscribed the ancient Georgian qvevri winemaking method on its list of intangible cultural heritage in 2013.

deeper.head: The oldest evidence
deeper.text: Excavations at the Neolithic villages of Gadachrili Gora and Shulaveri Gora, south of Tbilisi, found pottery with residues of grape wine dated to about 6000 BC, published in 2017. It is among the earliest chemical evidence of winemaking anywhere, and it underpins the claim of Georgia to eight thousand vintages.

deeper.head: Protected names
deeper.text: Georgia protects a set of appellations of origin, from Tsinandali and Mukuzani to Kindzmarauli and Khvanchkara, each tied to a delimited area, a grape or grapes and a style. The National Wine Agency registers them and checks the wines, and the list has grown since independence as more villages seek protection.

deeper.head: The red-fleshed Saperavi
deeper.text: The name Saperavi means dye or colour giver: its pulp is red, so even a short maceration gives a deep wine. It keeps high acidity in the heat of Kakheti, which lets it make both long-lived dry reds and the semi-sweet styles, in which the fermentation is stopped by chilling to keep natural sugar.

In Imereti, in the west, the wine traditionally ferments with only a small part of the skins and no stems, and the local vessel is called a churi; the wines are lighter and fresher than the amber whites of Kakheti, from Tsolikouri, Tsitska and Krakhuna.
